title: Everyday Verbs
description: The commonest verbs, in the short form people say out loud. They never change for who or when: saya makan, dia makan, kemarin kami makan.

items.english: to eat; to have a meal
items.cultureNote: Sudah makan? (Have you eaten?) is a friendly greeting, not an invitation. Sudah (I have) or Belum (not yet) are both fine answers.

items.registerNotes: Also for taking medicine: minum obat. Mau minum apa? (What would you like to drink?) is what a server or a host asks.

items.english: to go; to go out, leave
items.registerNotes: Before ke (to), pergi is often left out: Saya mau ke pasar (I'm going to the market). On its own it means to go out or leave: Dia sudah pergi (She's gone out).
Kapan datang? asks a visitor when they arrived. Terima kasih sudah datang is 'Thanks for coming'.

items.english: to go home, come home; to go back
items.registerNotes: Saya pulang dulu, ya (I'll head home now) is a common way to take your leave.
items.pitfallNote: Use pulang, not pergi ke rumah, for going home. It also covers going back to your own country: pulang ke Selandia Baru.

items.english: to sleep; to go to bed
items.registerNotes: Tidur siang is an afternoon nap, common in the heat of the day. Selamat tidur is 'good night' to someone going to bed.
Jam berapa bangun? asks what time someone gets up. With me-, membangun means to build.

items.english: to bathe, have a shower, wash
items.cultureNote: Most Indonesians mandi twice a day, morning and late afternoon, often by scooping water over themselves with a dipper (gayung) from a tank (bak mandi).

items.registerNotes: Written and formal Indonesian says membeli; beli is the everyday spoken form, polite enough for any shop. Beli di mana? (Where did you buy it?) is a common friendly question.
Membayar in writing. Bayar di mana? asks where to pay, and the answer is often Di kasir (at the till).
items.pitfallNote: There's no word for 'for': bayar makanan is 'pay for the food'.

items.registerNotes: Melihat in writing. Boleh lihat? is 'May I have a look?', and Lihat-lihat saja (Just looking) is what you tell a shop assistant.
Mendengar in writing; listening to music is dengar musik in speech, mendengarkan musik in writing. Maaf, saya tidak dengar is 'Sorry, I didn't catch that'.
Berbicara in writing; friends say ngomong. Bisa bicara bahasa Inggris? asks 'Can you speak English?'
Saya tidak tahu is 'I don't know'. In casual speech and messages it's often tau. The same word also means tofu.
items.pitfallNote: For knowing a person or a place, use kenal: Saya kenal dia (I know him).

items.registerNotes: Saya suka kopi is 'I like coffee', and Suka? asks 'Do you like it?'. In speech suka also means 'tend to': Dia suka terlambat (He's often late).
Tinggal di mana? (Where do you live? / Where are you staying?) is one of the first questions you'll be asked. Tinggal also means 'to be left': tinggal satu, only one left.
items.pitfallNote: Don't add me-: meninggal means 'to die'.

items.registerNotes: Bekerja in writing. Kerja di mana? (Where do you work?) is a standard small-talk question.
Saya belajar bahasa Indonesia is 'I'm learning Indonesian'.
items.pitfallNote: Belajar is learning; teaching is mengajar.

items.registerNotes: Menunggu in writing. Tunggu sebentar, ya (Just a moment, please) is heard everywhere.
items.pitfallNote: There's no word for 'for': tunggu saya is 'wait for me'.

items.registerNotes: Mencari in writing. Cari apa? (What are you looking for?) is what shopkeepers ask.
items.pitfallNote: c always sounds like the ch in 'church': cari is 'chah-ree', and kari is curry.
